catalog_quote: [p.75] Three degrees of stress have been traditionally distinguished for Finnish: a syllable may be primarily stressed, secondarily stressed or unstressed. ... Primary stress is invariably fixed to the word-initial syllable of a word; apparent exceptions will be dispelled below. Secondary stresses occur in longer than trisyllabic words, and they are not fully predictable. Usually, secondary stress falls on the third or the fourth syllable, and later in the word usually on every second syllable except the last one; however, secondary stress may fall on a final heavy syllable if the preceding syllable is light. Ultimately, where secondary stresses fall depends both on the segmental structure of syllables and on morphological structure (for details, see Karlsson 1983: 150–151). sweep_summary: Three title hits for Finnish. Two obtained and read (both via Internet Archive copy, the original hosts being dead): Elenbaas 1999 (Utrecht dissertation, full 232-page text, primary data) and Karttunen 2006 (author preprint of the Kaplan festschrift chapter). Both state fixed initial primary stress with quantity-sensitive alternating secondary stress (light-followed-by-heavy skipped, final light never stressed, final heavy optional), confirming the catalog's weight-hedged coding under Suomi, Toivanen & Ylitalo 2008; Elenbaas adds the detailed quantity/optionality/morphology conditions on secondary stress. Lehiste 1997 (De Gruyter, comparative Finnish/Finland Swedish/Stockholm Swedish prosody) is closed access (Unpaywall closed, De Gruyter bot-blocked, no HathiTrust/archive.org copy) and was not read; low priority since it is a comparative phonetic chapter and the catalog already rests on an authoritative open monograph. Nothing supersedes the catalog's deciding source.

new_statements.quote: In Finnish, the place of main stress is fixed. Main stress is on the initial syllable. Finnish has a quantity-sensitive stress system. Heavy syllables attract stress. CV is light, CVV, CVC, and CVVC are heavy. But regardless of the weight of the initial syllable, and that of the second syllable, main stress is on the initial syllable. [...] In Finnish, the second syllable never receives stress. There is an undominated constraint that forces the prosodic word to begin with main stress.
new_statements.citation: Elenbaas, Nine (1999). A unified account of binary and ternary stress: Considerations from Sentani and Finnish. PhD dissertation, Utrecht University (LOT). ISBN 90-5569-065-1.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 5 §5.5.1 'Main stress', p. 106 (secondary stress §5.5.2 pp. 106-108; summary §5.1 p. 95)
new_statements.reading: Primary stress is fixed on the word-initial syllable, insensitive to weight; secondary stress alternates from the left (odd-numbered syllables), never on a final light syllable, and is quantity-sensitive: a light odd-numbered syllable followed by a heavy syllable is skipped in favour of the heavy one (ternary patterns), final heavy syllables optionally stressed, with further morphologically conditioned variation. This is a first-hand statement based on the author's own elicited data verified with Finnish speakers; it agrees fully with the catalog's weight-hedged coding (fixed initial primary, weight-influenced and not fully predictable secondary).

new_statements.quote: Sanapainolla tarkoitetaan yksittäisen sanan sisäistä painotusta. Sanalla on pääpaino ja neli- tai useampitavuisella sanalla myös sivupaino. Suomessa sanan pääpaino on ensimmäisellä tavulla, oli tavu lyhyt tai pitkä. [...] Perustapauksessa tahtiyksikkö käsittää painollisen ja yhden painottoman tavun ja sivupaino lankeaa joka toiselle tavulle, ts. kolmannelle, viidennelle, seitsemännelle jne. tavulle (a). Sanan viimeinen tavu on yleensä painoton. Mikäli kuitenkin sivupaino osuisi lyhyelle tavulle, paino siirtyy tätä seuraavalle pitkälle tavulle (b).
new_statements.translation: Word stress means the stress internal to a single word. A word has a main stress, and a word of four or more syllables also a secondary stress. In Finnish the main stress of a word is on the first syllable, whether the syllable is short or long. [...] In the basic case the foot unit comprises a stressed and one unstressed syllable and secondary stress falls on every second syllable, i.e. on the third, fifth, seventh etc. syllable (a). The last syllable of a word is usually unstressed. If, however, secondary stress would land on a short syllable, the stress moves to the following long syllable (b).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Elenbaas 1999 statement (fixed initial primary, weight-insensitive; alternating quantity-sensitive secondary). Adds the morphological conditioning (compounds, inherently stressed suffixes such as -Oi-, case/possessive suffixes attracting stress leftward with free variation) and numeral stress. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field, so this is the reference-grammar statement that fills it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is always on the first syllable regardless of its length; secondary stress falls on every second syllable after it (3rd, 5th, 7th..), skipping to the next long syllable when it would land on a short one, which yields three- or four-syllable feet; the final syllable is normally unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Binary alternation from the left (3rd, 5th, 7th syllable) driven by speech rhythm and syllable length; a short syllable that would carry secondary stress is skipped in favour of the following long syllable (examples from Elenbaas 1999, Ogden 2001, F. Karlsson 1983); two stressed syllables never adjoin except in compounds (ˈmaan.ˌtie), where each member starts a new foot.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds allow adjacent stresses and each member starts a new foot; some derivational and inflectional morphemes carry inherent stress and take secondary stress even across a long syllable (suffix -Oi-: (ˈdo.ku.men).(ˌtoi.tiin)); case endings and possessive suffixes shift secondary stress to the syllable before them, with the length-based placement as a free alternative ((ˈsu.ku.lai).(ˌsel.la.ni) ~ (ˈsu.ku).(ˌlai.sel).(ˌla.ni)); numerals: multiplicative parts stress the first element (ˈkaksi ˌsataa), additive ones the second or both (ˌsata ˈkaksi; ˌtuhat ˈsata ~ ˈtuhat ˈsata); -kymmentä is reduced in speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe standard Finnish (VISK covers the standard language with occasional notes on spoken reductions such as viis.kyt; Elenbaas & Kager draw on Carlson 1978, Kager 1992, Hanson & Kiparsky 1996 and Elenbaas 1999, all on standard Finnish). No dialect-specific claims. Works 0 and 2 are the same grammar (Iso suomen kielioppi 2004; online VISK 2008 edition read for both).

new_statements.quote: In Finnish (Carlson 1978, Kager 1992, Hanson & Kiparsky 1996, Alber 1997, Elenbaas 1999) main stress falls on the word-initial syllable. Secondary stresses fall on every second syllable to the right (73a–d) [...] In (73f–h) we observe deviations from binary alternation in the form of local ternary intervals. When the second syllable to the right of a preceding stress is light and the third is heavy (that is, closed or long-voweled), secondary stress shifts rightward onto the heavy syllable. [p. 303:] Next, observe that secondary stress on a final heavy syllable is always optional, regardless of whether it is odd-numbered (76a, b) or even-numbered (76c, d) in the parity count.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author as the existing Elenbaas 1999 statement and the same facts: fixed initial primary stress, alternating quantity-sensitive secondary stress with light-skipping and optional final-heavy stress. Nothing new on placement; the OT analysis is the paper's contribution.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the word-initial syllable; secondary stress on every second syllable rightward, except that a light syllable followed by a heavy (closed or long-vowelled) syllable is skipped so the secondary stress lands on the heavy one, giving local ternary intervals; a final heavy syllable takes secondary stress only optionally.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Left-to-right binary trochaic alternation (périjä, répeàmä, érgonòmia, púhelìmenàni) with light-syllable skipping before a heavy syllable (mátemàtiikka, púhelimìstani, rákastajàttariànsa); analysed as Align-L >> *(LH) >> Parse-σ >> All-Ft-L with an undominated *Lapse; final heavy syllables optionally stressed (kúningàs ~ kúningas, rávintolàt ~ rávintòlat) via free ranking of Non-Finality.
new_statements.exceptions: Local ternary intervals when the second syllable after a stress is light and the third is heavy; optional secondary stress on word-final heavy syllables (both parities). Footnote 17 says the ranking simplifies the full one in Elenbaas 1999 (undominated *Clash, FtBin).

new_statements.quote: Suomessa sanan pääpaino on ensimmäisellä tavulla, oli tavu lyhyt tai pitkä. Toisaalta painotonkin tavu voi olla lyhyt tai pitkä. Sivupainon sijaintiin vaikuttaa kaksi fonologista tekijää: puherytmi ja tavujen pituus. Puherytmi perustuu suomessa kaksitavuiselle tahdille eli jalalle.
new_statements.translation: In Finnish the main stress of a word is on the first syllable, whether the syllable is short or long. On the other hand an unstressed syllable too can be short or long. Two phonological factors affect the position of secondary stress: speech rhythm and syllable length. Speech rhythm in Finnish is based on a two-syllable foot.

sources.citation: Anttila, Arto. 2017. Word stress in Finnish: Some new results. Handout, University of Utah Linguistics Colloquium, 16 Nov 2017 (12 pp., Stanford open PDF).
sources.quote: '(1) The stress rule (first approximation, Carlson 1978, Elenbaas and Kager 1999): (a) Primary stress falls on the initial syllable. (b) Secondary stress falls on every other syllable after that (c) except that a light syllable is skipped if the syllable after that is heavy (d) unless the heavy syllable is final in which case skipping is optional.' Notes the skipping clause 'leaks both ways' and shows intra-individual variation (fí.lo.sò.fìs.sa, ál.ler.gi.às.sa ~ ?ál.ler.gì.as.sa).

sources.citation: Anttila, Arto. 2007. Word stress in Finnish. Handout, LSA Annual Meeting, Anaheim, 4-7 January 2007 (14 pp., Stanford open PDF).
sources.quote: '(2) Primary stress is always initial. All the action is in secondary stress. (3) The general pattern (binarity): Stress every other syllable after primary stress ... (4) The special pattern (ternarity): Skip a light syllable if the syllable after that is heavy unless the heavy syllable is final in which case skipping is optional ... (5) Binary trochaic feet from left to right; main stress on the leftmost foot; heavy syllables must be stressed.'

sources.citation: Karttunen, Lauri (2006). The insufficiency of paper-and-pencil linguistics: The case of Finnish prosody. In Intelligent Linguistic Architectures: Variations on Themes by Ronald M. Kaplan, 287-300 (pages per Glottolog).
sources.quote: In general, Finnish prosody is trochaic with the main stress on the first syllable and a secondary stress on every other following syllable. Finnish also has a ternary stress pattern that surfaces in words where the stress would fall on a light syllable that is followed by a heavy syllable. A light syllable ends with a short vowel (ta); a heavy syllable ends with a coda consonant (jat, an) or a long vowel (kuu, aa) or a diphthong (voi, ei).

States that Finnish is trochaic with main stress on the first syllable, secondary stress on every other following syllable, and a ternary pattern where stress would fall on a light syllable followed by a heavy one (weight-driven secondary stress); lists Kiparsky's constraint 'Main Stress: The primary stress in Finnish is on the first syllable' (preprint p. 5, (4c)). An important phenomenon is the LH EFFECT: when the left-to-right scansion encounters a Light-Heavy sequence, the light syllable is skipped ... At the left edge of a word, the LH effect is superseded by the inviolable requirement that a word must have initial stress.'
